rationale: Both plans understand that this is a workflow and incentive problem, and both use champions or lighthouse projects, avoid mandates and retroactive migration, and measure time-to-reproduce. B offers sharp organisational insights: the PI problem, the 'two systems' tax, the funding-cycle cliff, and publication-workflow integration as the feature that wins PIs over. However, its sequencing stands up Git, Slurm or Kubernetes/Kubeflow, MLflow, JupyterHub and a versioned data store within weeks 3-4. That is unrealistic for a 30-day phase and sits awkwardly beside its own 'don't over-engineer' list. Its advice to delete laptop copies is heavy-handed. A is more internally coherent and feasible. It starts with a one-page concrete definition of 'reproducible', picks one beachhead workflow, and builds the thinnest convention: a repo per project, a pinned environment, a single run command and a REPRODUCE.md. It adds tracking and orchestration tools only when real pain appears. It ends with a cold reproducibility audit as both baseline metric and advocacy tool, and its 'do not build' list follows directly from that philosophy. A is the better-calibrated 90-day plan.
